item.title: What Does 2026 Mean for the Map in 2028?
item.description:
America’s political map looked pretty calcified — until last week.

Democrats’ surprising midterm wins across red states — including Scott Colom’s victory over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi — have raised new questions for both parties that will matter a lot for 2028 and beyond.

Was this all a blip, specific to this particular moment? Or could America’s political map be changing in a bigger way, putting longtime Republican strongholds in play for Democrats?

Tonight, let’s dive into the biggest question coming out of the midterms.

Since 2016, just six states have actually swung between Democratic and Republican presidential candidates. In the Senate, red-state Democrats and blue-state Republicans became endangered species. And the map of competitive House districts grew ever narrower.

But Democrats’ big Senate flips last week mostly came in states that haven’t backed their party for president in years.

“When you start losing Mississippi and Maine simultaneously, then you clearly have lost popular sentiment,” Newt Gingrich, the former House speaker, told me.

He would know. In 1994, he led his party to make enormous gains in the House, a “Republican revolution” that set the stage for the map we know today. And he believes that Democrats’ wins last week just might be the beginning of a rare political realignment, depending on how they govern.

“If the Democrats can discipline themselves to listen to the American people, they could create a new majority that could govern for quite a long time,” he said.

There is no guarantee, of course, that any wave election will become more than a one-off. In 1946, the year after Franklin D. Roosevelt’s death and Harry Truman’s ascent, Republicans swept Democrats out of the House and Senate — only to see their power ebb again two years later when Truman, a Democrat, won a full term.

And in 2006, Democrats captured both the House and the Senate as the public tired of George W. Bush, then deepened their control of government with the 2008 rise of President Barack Obama. Then, of course, came the “shellacking” of 2010, when Republicans picked up seats in the Senate and gained control of the House.

But sometimes, a wave election can signal the start of something more long-term.

Take 1964, when Lyndon B. Johnson, Democrat, won 44 states and Washington, D.C. It was a Democratic landslide. But a band of states in the Deep South backed Barry Goldwater, that year’s Republican presidential nominee, and those states have mostly stuck with Republicans ever since, especially when it comes to presidential elections.

And look at the presidential map in 1996. Two years after Gingrich first won power in the House, you can see the last gasps of Democratic dominance in Southern states like West Virginia, Arkansas and Tennessee — states that became seemingly impossible for the party to win when President Bill Clinton was no longer on the ballot.

Democrats believe they now have the opportunity to reimagine their party’s path to power, which in recent presidential elections has run through the “blue wall” states of Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. A party that can compete in the South — or even just in Texas, which has 40 electoral votes — has a lot more ways to win.

I called Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia, who believes that this is the moment for Democrats to go all in on winning in Southern states, which have not in recent years been seen as critical to what he called “the math of our majority.” Now, he said, they should be.

“The South is the fastest-growing region in the country,” Warnock said. “It’s the only region in the country where we’re seeing population growth for every age group. And when you look at the base of the Democratic Party and its most loyal voters, Black voters, the South is where the big and valiant struggle for our voices is being waged.”

Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky told me he thought red states that just elected Democratic governors, like Ohio and Iowa, could remain competitive in 2028.

“Democrats were looking in ’28 and ’32 at a shrinking map with very little margin of error,” he said. “Now they’re going to be able to go and campaign in states, lean on Democratic governors that have won in those states, and know how to turn out voters.”

It’s much too early to know what the 2028 map is going to look like. But the uncertainty about the nation’s political geography is new, and could shape the contest in unpredictable ways.

quote of the day

That was Hunter Patterson, a police dispatcher in Montgomery County, Texas. A “libertarian independent,” he said he usually voted Republican but no longer considered himself one after the party’s sharp turn to the right in recent years.

Patterson said he disagreed with James Talarico on many things, but still voted for him for Senate.

The question of what independent-minded voters like Patterson do in the future will go a long way to determining whether states like Texas snap back to red, or stay purple.

My colleague Sabrina Tavernise spoke with lots of them. Read her reporting.

CATCH ME UP

Jensen Huang, the embattled chief executive of the chip giant Nvidia, resigned, sending shock waves through the tech industry.

His downfall costs the A.I. boom one of its top backers, Ben Casselman writes.

Trump said that he would pull back Vice President JD Vance from potential peace talks with Iran, and that Vance’s time would be better spent focused on domestic fraud.

Will Democrats fight to impeach or investigate Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. with their new majorities? Or, Sheryl Gay Stolberg writes, will they try to work with him on areas where they can agree?

House Democrats faced a backlash after 11 of them missed a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Hospitals across the country are racing to keep millions of patients insured, and bracing for huge funding cuts, before new Medicaid work rules and guidelines begin in the new year.

Cities are employing a new strategy to delay the Trump administration’s effort to build ICE jails: using a lawsuit to stall the construction of immigration detention centers until Democrats take over Congress.

q+A

One Senate race has yet to be called: Alaska’s.

Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, is narrowly leading Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, and an analysis of ballots by The New York Times found that she is likely to prevail. But the state’s ranked-choice voting system means that tallying votes there is extra complicated.

My colleague Christine Zhang, a reporter on our Election Analytics team, has been watching the count closely, and is here with a quick update.

Christine, what’s happening in Alaska right now? Why is their count taking so long?

Alaska has reported 86 percent of the votes so far. The remaining ballots are mostly mail-in ballots, which need to be reviewed before being included in the count. It can also take a long time to transport mail ballots through the state’s remote, inaccessible regions. Officials will count ballots that arrive up to 10 days after Election Day, as long as they were postmarked by Nov. 3.

How much longer do officials there have to count?

They have until Nov. 18 to count all the remaining ballots. That’s also the date when ranked-choice tabulation will begin if the top candidates in the statewide races have not cleared the 50 percent threshold needed to win outright.

During this process, whoever is in last place will be eliminated, and the votes for that candidate will instead be awarded to each voter’s next choice still in the race. That goes on until two candidates are left, and the one with more votes wins.

OK. Is Nov. 18 when we might officially learn the winner of the race?

Well, there’s a chance that the Senate race could be called sooner, if it doesn’t go to ranked-choice tabulation at all. The remaining vote is from areas favorable to Peltola, so we’ll have to see how it goes in the days ahead. But yes, if the race is decided by ranked-choice tabulation, we will most likely know on Nov. 18.

in the states

In 2024, voters in states like Arizona and Missouri backed abortion-rights measures even as they supported candidates like President Trump who had celebrated the fall of Roe v. Wade.

This year, the reverse has happened. As Democratic candidates won statewide races, several high-profile conservative ballot measures prevailed. The dissonant results show that voters do not always move the same way all at once — even in a wave election.

California narrowly killed a measure for a wealth tax on billionaires.

Arizona handily passed a Republican-backed referendum to require transgender students to use bathrooms and locker rooms aligned with the sex listed on their birth certificates. Voters in three more states, including Colorado, passed similar measures.

Voters in seven states, including Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio, passed measures to ban noncitizen voting or require voter identification — ideas long pushed by conservative groups.

Two more Republican bright spots:

New England’s two Republican governors withstood the blue wave. Read about how they did it.

Paul LePage, the former governor of Maine, flipped a House seat in a rare midterm battleground win for Republicans.

ONE LAST THING

Bruce Giudici tried for years to win a seat on the board of supervisors in Calaveras County, Calif. Then he died. But his odds of winning the seat are looking better than ever.

On Aug. 30, his campaign said, he was out door-knocking when he fell. Giudici, who was 68, died the next day. His campaign pushed forward anyway, and its grass-roots politicking seems to have paid off: Giudici has posthumously received 57 percent of the vote in his race.

Taylor Robinson and Christine Zhang contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Had Urged Nvidia’s Jensen Huang to Fight for His Job
item.description:
President Trump called Jensen Huang on Tuesday, before the Nvidia chief stepped down amid a rapidly unfolding spy scandal, and urged him to keep fighting for his job, according to two people briefed on the conversation.

The call was the latest instance of Mr. Trump defending and protecting Mr. Huang, who had become a high-profile ally and an influential adviser on artificial intelligence. The president continued to back him to the end, even after U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that Mr. Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Nvidia announced on Thursday that Mr. Huang, who built the company into the world’s leading supplier of advanced A.I. chips, had been replaced as chief executive following revelations not just of the affair with the woman suspected of being a spy, but also another with one of his employees.

A representative for Mr. Huang did not provide a comment for this article. Neither Mr. Trump nor the White House responded to requests for comment about his call to Mr. Huang.

The president had been warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a Chinese citizen known as Alice Huang, whom intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.

Mr. Trump took no action either time, and brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China in May. In recent days, he has publicly praised Mr. Huang and expressed sympathy for him, saying in a social media post on Thursday that he was a “legend.”

The president’s advisers said he was blasé about the national security implications when told of the intelligence community assessments related to Mr. Huang. One aide said that Mr. Trump saw the episode mainly through the lens of adultery, and that the president dismissed the idea of Mr. Huang’s entanglement posing a threat to the country.

Mr. Trump saw Nvidia as essentially too big to fail, aides said. The company, one of the world’s largest by market capitalization, has played a vital role in the global economy and underpinned the president’s hopes for A.I. dominance over China.

Advisers to Mr. Trump gave several explanations for the way he had handled the matter, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive conversations.

Chief among them was that the president had invested greatly in Mr. Huang, whom he saw as a modern-day Henry Ford, leading in a technology that could define the century.

Mr. Trump viewed Nvidia’s fortunes as bound up with those of the U.S. economy and the stock market. When reports surfaced that the company’s board was considering removing Mr. Huang, Mr. Trump asked confidants what they thought would happen to the markets. He was worried that Mr. Huang’s ouster could cause a sharp downturn.

The president’s last-ditch effort to save Mr. Huang was a remarkable moment in a relationship that barely existed two years ago.

During Mr. Trump’s first term, Mr. Huang was nowhere on his radar. The Nvidia founder had no real presence in Washington. He did not lobby or give to campaigns, and showed little interest in politics. The Biden administration’s sweeping restrictions on chip exports forced Mr. Huang to be more attentive to Washington, but he still did far less politicking than his rivals. In contrast to other tech leaders, he did not attend Mr. Trump’s second inauguration.

With evident relish, Mr. Trump has told the story of first hearing Mr. Huang’s name. “Who the hell is he? What’s his name?” he has recalled to associates. “His name is Jensen Huang of Nvidia. I said, ‘What the hell is Nvidia?’”

By late 2024, Mr. Trump had learned that Mr. Huang was the indispensable man at the company that controlled at least 80 percent of the market for chips used to train the most advanced A.I. models. And Mr. Huang saw an opening to woo a president who demanded personal attention and responded to flattery.

In April 2025, Mr. Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a dinner at Mar-a-Lago with Mr. Trump and a group of tech and crypto donors. The president came away intrigued, and the more he learned, the more impressed he became, people who spoke with him at the time said. He was told again and again that the A.I. boom ran almost entirely through Nvidia. “You’re taking over the world, Jensen,” Mr. Trump would later tell him.

Mr. Huang offered something the president had failed to get in his first term and hoped to achieve in his second. During his first administration, Mr. Trump had pledged to bring back coal and steel jobs. But those industries never returned to their old strength.

In a second term, A.I. offered another route to the reindustrialization of the United States that Mr. Trump had promised voters. He came to believe that the rush to build data centers, and their enormous appetite for electricity, could produce a manufacturing revival and keep an otherwise shaky economy running hot, people close to him said. To the president, that made the leaders of the A.I. companies the most valuable executives in the country, and Mr. Huang perhaps the most valuable of them all.

Mr. Huang played into that savior role. In 2025, he said Nvidia would produce up to $500 billion of A.I. infrastructure in the United States. He also praised the president lavishly.

“America’s unique advantage that no country could possibly have is President Trump,” he said that July. He traveled with Mr. Trump to the Persian Gulf in May 2025, where the president announced deals for Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates to buy Nvidia chips. He provided the kind of deal-making headlines that Mr. Trump craved.

Mr. Huang had persuaded Mr. Trump that Nvidia should sell its chips as widely as possible, so that the world would build on U.S., rather than Chinese, technology. David Sacks, the White House’s A.I. and crypto czar, backed him. The two men helped persuade Mr. Trump to plant himself on the unpopular side of a major issue for the populist right.

China hawks on the MAGA right, including Stephen K. Bannon, wanted chip sales to China banned outright. But Mr. Trump sided with Mr. Huang and his billionaire counterparts leading other tech companies, including OpenAI, Meta and SpaceX.

At Mr. Huang’s urging, Mr. Trump allowed Nvidia to sell certain models of its chips to China under an unusual arrangement in which the federal government took 15 percent, and later 25 percent, of the revenue. Critics raised legal questions and warned that national security was being sold out. Administration officials privately marveled at how much sway Mr. Huang seemed to have with the president.

Some U.S. officials had worried about Mr. Huang long before the spy scandal broke into the open this fall. They saw him as, at best, naïve and careless in his dealings with Chinese executives and local officials, with whom he kept close ties. Some wondered how he could possibly have been oblivious to Ms. Huang’s possible connections to Chinese intelligence.

But Mr. Trump was never likely to share in those national security concerns. While he has used bellicose campaign rhetoric against China — he has accused Beijing of “raping” the American economy and made that line of attack a focus of his 2016 presidential campaign — he has never been a China hawk in any conventional sense.

Throughout the president’s terms, his aggressive posture on China has been limited to trade. And even there he has repeatedly shown he would rather cut a deal with Xi Jinping, the country’s leader, than engage in a protracted trade war.

Unlike some of his predecessors, Mr. Trump has largely ignored Beijing’s human rights abuses. Asked in 2020 why he had not imposed sanctions over the mass detention of Uyghurs in Xinjiang, he said, “Well, we were in the middle of a major trade deal.”

People close to the president say that in private, he has questioned why the United States would ever go to war over Taiwan.

To dramatize his disregard for the small island nation, Mr. Trump has been known to hold up a teaspoon to lunch guests at his golf club and say, “This is Taiwan.”

item.title: Van Hollen Says He Will Challenge Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
item.description:
Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced on Thursday that he would challenge Senator Chuck Schumer of New York for majority leader, setting up a clash among Democrats just as they were celebrating their new majority and planning for a takeover of Congress in January.

The move by Mr. Van Hollen, a progressive Democrat elected to the Senate in 2016 after seven terms in the House representing the Washington, D.C. suburbs, comes as some Democratic senators and activists have called for an alternative to Mr. Schumer, a moderate whom they regard as too tied to the party establishment to lead a newly energized party forward in the next Congress.

Mr. Van Hollen, who is also said to be weighing a run for president in 2028, had emerged as the favorite to challenge Mr. Schumer for the post and had expressed increasing willingness to do so in recent days.

Senate Democrats are scheduled to vote behind closed doors on Dec. 1 to determine who will be their leader when their party takes the Senate majority on Jan. 4.

“I think there is a big appetite for change within the Democratic Caucus,” Mr. Van Hollen said in an interview before the announcement. “I think people want to have a system of much more meaningful input, and that’s going to be even more important now that we have this large majority.”

His announcement came as Mr. Schumer and his allies reiterated that the New York Democrat had commitments of support from well over the majority of Senate Democrats needed to re-elect him as leader.

In a statement, Mr. Schumer said that he welcomed “a discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead.”

“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader,” he said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

Mr. Schumer oversaw the Senate Democratic campaign effort that has flipped at least eight Senate seats, with the Democrat Scott Colom on Wednesday called as the winner in the Mississippi Senate race. The Alaska Senate race result has not been called, but the Democrat Mary Peltola is slightly ahead there.

Despite that success, some in the ranks of Senate Democrats have called for a broad discussion of party leadership going forward and a debate over the agenda the party should pursue.

Other Democrats say that the leadership fight is distracting from the stunning victory Democrats recorded on Nov. 3 and hurting their preparation for January.

“We were at 47-53 and now we are at 55, 56,” said Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania and a strong supporter of Mr. Schumer. He added: “I don’t understand why that’s a conversation.”

Other Democrats have noted the contrast of Senate Republicans returning their leadership team without a challenge after losing at least 8 seats while Democrats are embroiled in a showdown despite their win.

Mr. Van Hollen, 67, is the child of a diplomat and was elected to the House in 2002 after entering the race as an underdog in a very competitive primary while serving in the Maryland legislature.

In the House, he became a close ally to Speaker Nancy Pelosi and a leading voice on budget issues. In 2008, he led the House campaign effort as Democrats expanded their majority when Barack Obama was elected president and also led the campaign team in 2010.

Mr. Van Hollen was seen as a potential future speaker in the House, but that prospect seemed far-off given Ms. Pelosi’s hold on the office. When Barbara Mikulski of Baltimore was set to retire from the Senate in 2016, he sought her seat and won. Given his experience, Senate Democrats immediately put him in charge of their campaign organization.

In the Senate, Mr. Van Hollen has focused on budget issues and foreign policy. He has been an outspoken proponent of cutting off money for the war against Iran.

Progressive activists have urged that Mr. Schumer, 75, face a challenge to remaining in the position. Donors and organizations including MoveOn, Indivisible and the Working Families Party plan to back and mobilize members on behalf of Mr. Van Hollen. They are threatening to back primary challenges against any Democratic senator up for re-election in 2028 who does not come out in support of him.

Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont who aligns with Democrats, has said he would oppose Mr. Schumer and encouraged Mr. Van Hollen to become a candidate.

Mr. Schumer and his allies have been adamant that he has more than enough votes to hold the position. But secret ballot leadership votes can be unpredictable. Some senators have refrained from going public with their support to avoid coming under pressure from those urging that Mr. Schumer be deposed.

Mr. Van Hollen says he was not deterred by Mr. Schumer’s claim on the votes to prevail.

“Circumstances change,” he said. “It is one thing to have someone’s support when you’re the only choice. I think a little democracy in the Senate Democratic Caucus is a good thing.”

Lisa Lerer and Reid J. Epstein contributed reporting.

item.title: After Influence Peddling Claims, White House Restricts Lobbyist Meetings
item.description:
President Trump’s new White House chief of staff is wasting little time trying to differentiate himself from his predecessor.

The office of Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump aide who was elevated to chief of staff last week after Susie Wiles was ousted, issued a memo forbidding White House staff from meeting with lobbyists about policy issues on the building’s grounds without prior approval, according to a person who received the memo and was not authorized to disclose it.

“No President in history has fought more relentlessly, selflessly or courageously for the American People than President Trump,” reads the memo. “Following his example, White House staff are expected to dedicate their time unwaveringly to the working people of the nation.”

The White House did not respond to questions on Thursday night about the memo and what prompted it.

The memo, which was posted on social media by a podcaster allied with Mr. Trump on Thursday and also reported by Politico, follows claims last week by a former top Trump administration health adviser who accused the White House of catering to lobbyists and their clients raising significant funds for the president’s political groups and projects.

Calley Means, a prominent figure in the Make America Healthy Again movement, blamed Ms. Wiles.

Mr. Means, who resigned last month from the Department of Health and Human Services, contended that Ms. Wiles tilted administration health policy to favor corporate donors who hired well-connected lobbyists over ordinary Americans.

He specifically cited Ballard Partners, a lobbying firm where Ms. Wiles once worked, and Ms. Wiles’s daughter, Katie Wiles, who is a partner at the lobbying firm Continental Strategy.

“So if you’re a special interest and you want to get something done, the secret’s out,” Mr. Means said during an interview on The Joe Rogan Experience podcast. “You pay Susie’s daughter, and it was openly discussed when they had a client.”

The White House pushed back on the claims and has said that Katie Wiles did not discuss her business with her mother.

Continental Strategy has said that Katie Wiles does not lobby the U.S. government on behalf of any clients.

Susie Wiles did not respond to requests for comment on Thursday night.

Ballard Partners and its founder, Brian Ballard, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Thursday night.

But in a statement posted on social media on Sunday, Mr. Ballard said his firm’s interactions with Ms. Wiles as chief of staff were “limited and have been the exception, not the rule.”

Mr. Ballard has helped facilitate access to the president and his team for clients who have donated to the Trump-backed super PAC, the White House ballroom project and other projects favored by Mr. Trump. Those clients have sometimes benefited from changes in administration policy.

It is a far cry from 2016, when Mr. Trump ran as a Washington outsider promising to “drain the swamp.”

Mr. Miller started working for Mr. Trump during that campaign.

The podcaster who posted the memo, Benny Johnson, called it “a marked break” from Ms. Wiles’s leadership “and a signal that there is a massive crackdown coming.”

The memo requires Mr. Trump’s staff to receive approval from the White House Counsel’s Office for meetings in the White House complex with registered lobbyists.

Staff are asked to refer lobbyist inquiries to the Office of Public Liaison, the memo instructs, calling the office “the primary point of contact for engagement with external stakeholders.”

The memo nonetheless leaves wiggle room for special interests. Lobbyists could meet staff at venues Mr. Trump frequents outside of the White House complex, like his Mar-a-Lago resort and golf clubs. And many corporate executives have direct relationships with Mr. Trump, independent of their lobbyists.

item.title: Burgers, Boycotts and the Ad That Divided an Ohio Community
item.description:
The first time someone called P.J. Marley’s in protest, a 16-year-old employee picked up.

From the host stand of the beloved burger joint, he could see the tranquil town square of Medina, Ohio, with its gazebo, twinkle lights and flapping American flags. But on the phone, the caller was screaming.

“They said something,” the teen told his manager afterward, “about pedophiles?”

He could not remember everything the caller said, but he remembered that word, the one that so many people would use to insult the restaurant in the coming weeks.

“Never dining there, vile pedophile supporters,” a woman from a nearby county wrote on Facebook.

“Gross that they chose to give pedophile protectors a platform,” a local woman posted.

The onslaught began in late October, when the Ohio Republican Party announced that a group of candidates who were traveling the state in a big red bus would stop at P.J. Marley’s on the Saturday before the election. One of them, Vivek Ramaswamy, who was running for governor, had just released an ad in which the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, called her a liar.

Left unsaid was that when Ms. Acton was 12, her stepfather was charged with raping her, and her mother took the stepfather’s side.

Patty and Jon Stahl, the P and J behind P.J. Marley’s, had agreed to host the candidates before the much-criticized ad was released. They were known around town for raising four sons, volunteering in the local schools and transforming a 122-year-old bank into a tavern. They thought the ad was in poor taste. But as small-business Republicans, they believed in Mr. Ramaswamy’s pitch that he could lower property taxes without harming schools, and thought he could find a way to bring down their rising electric bills.

The couple insisted that holding an event for the Republican ticket was not about taking a side; they would have agreed to host Democrats, too, they said. “People were saying, ‘Oh, you’re giving Vivek a platform,’” Mr. Stahl said. “I looked at it as he was giving us a platform.”

But as the ad kept airing and the calls kept coming, what had felt like a good decision for their business and for civil discourse had instead become yet another battle in America over which side had the moral high ground.

The politicians and pundits who obsessed over the ad and its meaning would move on once the election was over. But as the uproar in Medina would show, the wounds it exposed would not easily heal.

Other businesses that had agreed to hold events for Mr. Ramaswamy were canceling. The Stahls needed to decide if they would, too.

“Hi Patty, I know it’s been a while,” Stacey Bene typed. She’d just seen a Facebook post about how the candidates were coming to P.J. Marley’s. She’d taken Jazzercise classes from Mrs. Stahl more than a decade earlier, and had said, “I know the owners here” every time she returned to P.J. Marley’s for a bacon burger.

Now, in hopes of persuading Mrs. Stahl to back out of hosting Mr. Ramaswamy, she was going to tell her something she rarely spoke about. In a private Facebook message, she wrote, “I was raped at the age of 14.”

Throughout the election season, the subject of physical and sexual abuse had felt almost inescapable in Ohio’s 7th District. In the congressional race, there were ads accusing Representative Max Miller, a Republican, of abusing his ex-wife and toddler, and ads in which he denied the allegations. In the Senate race, there were ads accusing the Republican incumbent, Jon Husted, of taking money from associates of Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex offender who died in jail.

But it was Mr. Ramaswamy’s ad that bothered Mrs. Bene, a retired social worker, the most, she said in an interview.

“I cannot separate you from the messages you are allowing to be spread at your facility,” she wrote to Mrs. Stahl.

It felt as if everyone in town were taking sides. Loyal customers were declaring they’d never again set foot in P.J.’s or the Stahls’ second restaurant. Conservatives who had never been to their establishments said they would now seek them out. A woman whose daughters both worked at P.J. Marley’s for years called for a boycott, which led someone else to call for white liberal women to be deported. A prominent Democrat who knew Mr. Stahl well defended him on Facebook, saying, “remember that people are more than their politics.”

The Stahls deleted every negative comment posted to their social media pages, and remained publicly silent.

Then the county Democrats announced plans for a protest outside the restaurant. In Medina County, where 62 percent of residents had voted for President Trump in 2024, Democrats were accustomed to being outnumbered.

Kellie Biegel, who lives around the corner from P.J. Marley’s, had been in a decade-long feud with her neighbor. The more Trump signs her neighbor acquired, the more pro-liberal signs Ms. Biegel put up.

One day this summer, she realized that all of her neighbor’s signs were gone. Ms. Biegel asked her to come over. They hugged. Hoping to ease the years of tension, she did not bring up politics.

But when Mr. Ramaswamy arrived in town on Oct. 31, Ms. Biegel knew where she would be.

The town square, which had served as a backdrop for a Gilmore Girls festival and a few rom-com movies, was filled with about 200 protesters. A video truck displayed an image of Mr. Ramaswamy and the question, “What kind of man runs this ad?”

Most of the protesters stuck to the square, where a massive sign declared, “KINDNESS WILL WIN.”

But Ms. Biegel joined a group near P.J. Marley’s back patio, shouting directly at customers.

“There they are,” she yelled as she livestreamed. “Pedophile supporters!”

Every seat inside P.J. Marley’s was filled. Some customers said they had come to hear the candidates; others just wanted to show support for the Stahls.

The couple had taught their sons that when you make a commitment, you stick to it. They planned to put out a statement expressing their belief in free speech and open dialogue, and saying that candidates and customers of all beliefs were welcome in their restaurant.

But after more and more disparaging messages dinged on their phones, they never posted it.

“Nothing we say at this point is going to make them happy,” Mr. Stahl said.

Inside the restaurant, he could not see the protesters. Ramaswamy aides had papered over the front windows with campaign signs. The thick walls of the former bank stopped the protesters from being heard. But every time an employee stepped outside, they got screamed at, too.

Anthony Buchanan, a bartender at the restaurant, stepped out through a side door to get fresh air. One protester kept yelling to him, “How can you work for them?”

Mr. Buchanan thought of what he could have snapped back: “If you’re honestly asking me that, you’re not aware of the way that life is. I’m a third-grade teacher. I work two jobs. I’m just trying to get my money.”

Instead, he went back inside and served craft beers while the candidates made speeches about the dangers of what would come if Republicans were not elected.

At 5 a.m. on the day after the election, Mr. Stahl grabbed his phone from his bedside table and checked the results.

Democrats had swept nearly all the statewide races in Ohio. None had flipped Medina County, although Mr. Ramaswamy had won it by a much smaller margin than Mr. Trump in 2024.

It had been nearly two weeks since the calls and messages started coming to P.J. Marley’s, and they had not stopped, even after the event was over. But the Stahls did not regret their decision. Their business had not appeared to suffer, and in their minds, they had shown everyone that they would not be bullied.

It did bother Mr. Stahl, though, how many customers and acquaintances had disparaged him online without ever directly talking to him.

Then again, he’d stopped talking back. Once he’d decided not to post a statement, he had not replied to a single message or email.

After getting out of bed, he took his phone to a chair in his living room and searched for a video of Mr. Ramaswamy’s concession speech.

“It was a tough race,” Mr. Ramaswamy said. “It was bitter at times, in both directions.”

But now it was time, he went on, “to bring Ohio together.”

Then Mr. Stahl watched Ms. Acton.

“The healing begins today,” she said. “We must never give up on one another.”

On Facebook, there was a new message notification.

“Oh well,” someone had written. “You ruined your business over a loser!”

Mr. Stahl tapped the name of sender and clicked block.

Kitty Bennett contributed research

item.title: The Christian Right Lost Big in the Elections. Where Does It Go Next?
item.description:
The Christian right suffered a crushing defeat in last week’s midterm elections, plunging the movement into frustration and uncertainty as it reels from its biggest losses since reaching new levels of power with President Trump.

Over the last decade, conservative Christians have hitched their ambitions to Mr. Trump’s, defending his leadership to advance their own goals, particularly around abortion. His causes in turn became theirs as they wove themselves into the MAGA coalition and infused its politics into the American church.

Now, his losses are theirs, too. The election results suggest that the movement’s grip inside Mr. Trump’s party has weakened, and religious conservatives are scrambling to regroup ahead of the 2028 presidential contest.

“What does the Christian right have today?” said Terry Schilling, president of American Principles Project, a political advocacy group that has worked to defeat transgender rights measures. “We could have been actually passing laws that would have protected our kids, but instead we got the Iran war.”

Christian activists like Mr. Schilling said the Trump administration gave them few successes over the past two years beyond some executive orders, including one establishing the White House Faith Office and another on “anti-Christian bias.”

“There’s no signature achievement. There’s nothing,” Mr. Schilling said. “We squandered an opportunity.”

Already, the Christian right is pivoting to emphasize affordability as essential to its vision for the American family.

It is a recognition that the movement is competing with an energized religious left that helped win elections last week with a moral argument — one that emphasized protesting ICE and restoring cuts to the social safety net that Republicans pushed through last year as part of Mr. Trump’s domestic policy law.

Senator Josh Hawley, the Missouri Republican who has championed what he has referred to as Christian nationalism, repeatedly mentioned needing to care for the poor in an interview on Thursday.

“Making sure people can afford to have a child or get married or buy a home or pay for their health care — these are things Christians care about. They are rooted in the Gospel,” he said.

He blamed low turnout by conservative Christian voters for the sweeping losses, and he urged Republicans to take more seriously the concerns of evangelical and Catholic voters who oppose abortion. He cited as an example the fact that Planned Parenthood, which provides abortions, still receives federal funding.

“The party’s focus has really got to change,” he said.

The election losses stung not only because of their scale, but also because many came in states where the Christian right had long been a political force. From Iowa to Kansas to South Carolina, causes that had previously mobilized the movement’s voter turnout machine, like opposition to abortion and support for Israel, played a minimal role as voters rebelled against rising costs and the war with Iran.

In Georgia, a hotbed of evangelical organizing, Democrats gained control of the governor’s office and the state House of Representatives. Even in Mississippi, ground zero in the legal fight that led to Roe v. Wade being overturned, a Democrat who supports reproductive rights unseated one of the anti-abortion coalition’s longtime advocates in the Senate.

The religious symbolism was equally powerful, as a large cohort of voters played a notable role in rejecting Mr. Trump’s agenda. The religious makeup of the next Congress is shifting to include eight Democrats who are Muslim and nine who are Christian pastors and seminarians.

An analysis from a new progressive political group, Evangelicals for A Better Future, found that the more Christian a county was, the more Democratic it voted in 2026 compared with 2024. Many of the counties with the most significant shifts have large Latino populations.

Most pointedly, Texas, the state whose Republican leaders pushed perhaps the most aggressive right-wing Christian agenda in the country, elected a Democratic senator, James Talarico, who motivated voters in part with his own progressive Christianity.

Conservative Christians earned a few victories. Voters in four states chose to bar transgender athletes from competing on female sports teams. In Idaho, where a total abortion ban is in effect, voters rejected a measure to restore abortion rights until fetal viability, the standard set in Roe. But in Virginia and Nevada, voters chose to enshrine abortion rights into their state constitutions.

Mr. Trump was elected two years ago with what many of his supporters saw as a divine mandate, and he promised to give Christians enhanced access to the White House. That resulted in photo ops and prayer services in the West Wing, but not in desired policy shifts, such as a ban on abortion medications.

In recent months, American adults lost significant confidence in President Trump’s ability to make good decisions about the economy, immigration and foreign policy, according to the Pew Research Center; that drop applied even among white evangelicals, long among Mr. Trump’s most ardent supporters.

By October, while they remained the only religious group largely pleased with Mr. Trump’s performance, even their approval had dropped to 58 percent from 78 percent.

“If you don’t go to ask for everyone’s vote, you are not going to get everyone’s vote,” said Kristan Hawkins, founder and president of Students for Life, an anti-abortion group.

At the same time, the Christian right lost figureheads old and new, with late Senator Lindsey Graham’s unexpected death in July and Charlie Kirk’s assassination last year.

Mr. Kirk, an evangelical Christian, inspired young conservative voters and managed to tie together the Trump coalition’s social and economic ambitions. At the 2024 Republican National Convention, he spoke about the skyrocketing price of owning a home and said young people couldn’t afford to have children. The American dream was a reality only for the rich, Mr. Kirk said, but Mr. Trump was on a mission to rescue them.

“Republicans failed to address that,” Ms. Hawkins said, signaling the potential focus of conservative Christian activists moving forward.

“Had Charlie not been assassinated, do I think things probably would have gone differently?” she asked of the midterm election results. “Yeah, I do.”

The movement’s leaders are looking for champions to take up the mantle. Vice President JD Vance, a Roman Catholic long seen as a front-runner to succeed Mr. Trump, has tried to distance himself from the president’s decisions on the Iran war.

Senator Hawley proposed an hour of fasting and prayer in December.

“For Christians who are dismayed as I am by the results of this election, right now is the time to pray and to ask yourself, ‘What am I supposed to do for the future of the country?’” he said. “That’s what I’m doing right now.”

The National Association of Christian Lawmakers, founded in 2019 to advance conservative Christian values and policy among elected officials, held its own three-day fast this week.

Jason Rapert, the group’s president, sees both Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth as “bright shining stars.”

Mr. Rapert dismissed the idea that American voters had rejected the goal of building a Christian country, summing up the losses as a failure to get out the conservative Christian vote. Already, his group is mobilizing followers against a new set of political targets.

He posted a 16-page letter on the group’s website, nine pages of which were devoted to “The Danger of Islam,” including an extensive list of the names of newly elected Muslim Americans around the country.

But the Christian right now faces an awakened religious opposition that is unwilling to tolerate Mr. Trump’s agenda and anti-Islamic rhetoric.

Two years ago it would have been almost impossible to imagine last Tuesday’s results, said Bishop Mariann Budde, the Episcopal bishop of Washington, who pleaded with Mr. Trump to “have mercy” the day after his inauguration last January.

This week she was cautiously optimistic.

“I’m grateful that Christians and other people of many faiths came together to fundamentally change the trajectory of our country’s future,” she said.

Still, she added, “We have a lot of work to do.”

item.title: ‘I Had to Have Faith’: How a Democrat Defied Long Odds in Mississippi’s Senate Race
item.description:
Barely more than a year ago, Scott Colom sat at the kitchen table at his parents’ house not far from his own home in northeastern Mississippi, using his lunch breaks from his job as district attorney to call potential donors.

Mississippi hadn’t had a Democratic senator since the 1980s. It hadn’t had a Black senator since the 1880s. But Mr. Colom made his pitch.

The response, in the recollection of his mother, Dorothy Colom, was typically a one-two beat:

You sound impressive.

You can’t win.

“It was just the two of us,” she said in an interview this week at her home in Columbus, Miss. “And my role was just to write down what the donors said.”

Now Mr. Colom, 43, is Mississippi’s senator-elect — and at the top of the list of Democrats whose unlikely wins in the midterm elections reordered the balance of power in Washington and scrambled longstanding preconceptions about who can win where.

A seventh-generation Mississippian descended from an enslaved woman, Mr. Colom (pronounced kuh-LOAM) defeated Cindy Hyde-Smith — the Republican incumbent who had single-handedly denied him a chance at a lifetime appointment as a federal judge three years before, blocking his nomination by President Joseph R. Biden Jr.

He wound up running for her seat, campaigning for more than a year before anybody but the most perceptive or optimistic Democrats believed he had a shot.

It frustrated Mr. Colom. But in the end, he said, it wasn’t all bad.

“It was good that it didn’t get attention too early,” he told The New York Times during the waning days of the campaign. “It made me earn it.”

“Throughout this campaign, there were many times where I had to have faith,” he said on Wednesday night in his victory speech at Tougaloo College, a historically Black school on the northern edge of Jackson, Miss., the state capital. “There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone. They did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith.”

Before his win in the primary in March, before a viral ad that introduced him to the world and before the last-minute assistance of senators and former presidents, Mr. Colom just kept making calls and his mother just kept taking notes.

You don’t have a chance.

But send me your bio?

Mr. Colom and his twin brother, Andrew, were born in 1982 to a power couple of Columbus, a small, majority-Black city near the Alabama state line.

His father, Wilbur Colom, was a lawyer, an entrepreneur and a collector of stone sculptures from Zimbabwe. In the 1960s, he was a civil rights activist. In the ’70s and ’80s, he was a Republican — working on Ronald Reagan’s presidential transition team and the Senate campaigns of Haley Barbour and Thad Cochran. He ran for state treasurer in ’87 and said Black people should stop just giving their votes to Democrats. “I think Black Democrats should be ashamed of themselves,” he told the Clarion Ledger newspaper that year.

His mother, Dorothy Colom, always a Democrat, met her husband on a Saturday night in the library at the Antioch School of Law in Washington, D.C. She was a lawyer, too, before she ran for a seat on the bench, losing two races before winning her third. She was the district’s first Black chancery judge and retired in 2018 after almost a quarter century.

The twins licked campaign mailers for their mother and politicked at county fairs with their father. They hit back-to-back home runs in Little League and took violin lessons. They played pool at the Boys and Girls Club and went to vacation Bible school. They had summer reading, and their mother made them write reports.

“My dad was definitely the bad cop; my mom was definitely the good cop,” Andrew Colom said in an interview. “He’s the one saying, ‘You can do better.’ She’s the one saying, ‘I know how hard you try.’ And you need both of those.”

At Columbus High School, Scott Colom loved basketball and dreamed of being the next Michael Jordan. He was competitive and worked hard; he was also 5-foot-9. On a winning team, he was not one of the better players — but was, according to his coach, Sammy Smith, one of the most valuable. “He was a mental, emotional — if you will — spiritual leader,” said Adam Garner, a teammate and lifelong friend.

Mr. Colom attended Millsaps College, a small liberal arts school in Jackson. He played three seasons of basketball and double-majored in English and history. After graduation, he moved to Guyana, teaching English for a nonprofit called World Teach.

At the University of Wisconsin Law School, he interned with the Justice Department and with the chief prosecutor for the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in Tanzania. He graduated cum laude in 2009 and was picked to be one of the student speakers at the ceremony.

He delivered a paean to his parents and a call to action to his generation.

“We enter a world with many problems, a world with great uncertainty,” he said. “But we are no longer observers of these problems. We are participants. For we have the tools to make a difference, the power to leave our mark on the world.

“I have no doubt that we are ready for our moment in history.”

Mr. Colom turned down a lucrative job at a big-time law firm in Chicago, his mother said, and came home.

He would later talk to a friend about the “irreplaceability” of being close to family. He knew his father was keeping his firm open with the hope he would return. “He said he could make a difference here,” Ms. Colom said.

In the first few years of the 2010s, he was a lawyer at a nonprofit, the Mississippi Center for Justice, working to stop what he saw as the insidious spread of poverty predators like payday lenders.

He became the youngest and first Black judge in the Lowndes County justice court and then the first Black city prosecutor in Columbus.

And he wrote regular columns for the local newspaper.

In The Commercial Dispatch, he wrote about friends and mentors, local businesses and the importance of talking to one’s neighbors. He wrote about reality TV (“Nothing is in fact real”) and about race relations (“I believe our children will one day live in a fully integrated society”).

He started to write, too, about politics.

The Tea Party, he wrote in 2011, “should not be viewed as a singular moment in history but a part of a larger American tradition.”

He continued: “Civic and political engagement have been healthy for our democracy. Effective self-government takes effort and conviction.”

He noted with interest the “anti-establishment message” of a minor Republican candidate for governor, Ron Williams, who argued that the political status quo was dividing white and Black voters so the “working men and women of Mississippi won’t vote as Mississippians.”

Mr. Colom concurred: “The populist message probably won’t be enough to get Williams past the Republican primary, but I think Williams has identified an issue boiling below the surface,” he wrote.

And he remarked on a rock-bottom moment for Democrats in Mississippi. He charted the party’s decades-long decline — starting in 1964, when Barry Goldwater became the first Republican presidential candidate to win the state since Reconstruction, and accelerating in 1978, when Mr. Cochran became the first Republican elected statewide in more than a century.

By 2011, Republicans controlled nearly everything.

“A political party is made up of people, folks with different agendas, interests and goals,” Mr. Colom wrote. “Getting people organized enough to do anything is difficult. And, in many ways, the state Democratic Party has to be rebuilt from the ground up.

“Yet, the Democratic Party must find leaders willing to do this.”

The headline of the column: “The future of the MS Dem Party.”

Mr. Colom will be a senator because he is not a federal judge. And he is not a federal judge because of Ms. Hyde-Smith.

He had been elected district attorney in 2015 in a majority-white district, beating an incumbent who had been in office since 1989. “A David and Goliath situation,” said Cheikh Taylor, a Mississippi state representative and the chairman of the state Democratic Party.

He was a populist Democrat who was also a progressive prosecutor.

“If we send a young person to jail for drugs, it may seem like you’re tough,” he said in a campaign stop that summer, according to The Commercial Dispatch. “But five to six years later, they’ve got a felony and they can’t find a job.”

As D.A., Mr. Colom at times personally prosecuted the cases involving the most egregious offenses while also prioritizing leniency for first-time, nonviolent crimes. In his first re-election bid, in 2019, he ran unopposed.

During his second term, Mr. Colom was asked by the Biden administration if he would consider a lifetime appointment as a federal judge. “It wasn’t something I had been dreaming about,” Mr. Colom told The Times this fall. “But talking to my mom, and the stability it would have brought with my family, I decided to go for it.”

He labored to secure bipartisan backing, including from Representative Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, a mentor and powerful Black Democrat, as well as two former Republican governors.

But Senate tradition says the home-state senators of judicial nominees can block confirmation hearings for candidates they object to, and Ms. Hyde-Smith did so.

Mr. Colom’s interview with the senator, no more than 15 minutes on a video call, felt to him perfunctory. “The interview of somebody that got their mind made up,” he said in an interview.

In rejecting Mr. Colom, Ms. Hyde-Smith cited contributions he had received from the liberal megadonors George and Alex Soros and a statement he had signed with more than 70 other progressive prosecutors in 2021 saying they did not support the criminalization of medical professionals or parents who help a transgender child get gender-affirming care.

The snub did not make him want revenge, he said. It did, however, make him look more carefully at Ms. Hyde-Smith’s record.

She had, for instance, voted in 2021 against a bipartisan infrastructure law — the largest infusion of federal infrastructure money in more than a decade, helping to shore up projects across Mississippi and accelerate restoration of the Amtrak railroad line along the Gulf Coast. It was something the state’s other Republican senator, Roger Wicker, had helped pass.

She was also in lock step with Trump administration policies “causing pain to people,” he said.

“I said, ‘Listen, somebody’s got to fight back against this,’” Mr. Colom told The Times.

He announced his Senate candidacy in September 2025.

“As a Christian, I forgive Cindy Hyde-Smith. I truly do. I have to,” he said in his first interview, on the podcast of The Commercial Dispatch. “But as a Mississippian, I’m frustrated about the way she votes.”

Months into this campaign, though, after so many lukewarm responses to all the kitchen-table calls, Mr. Thompson got on a group video call with Mr. Colom. The message was stark: The cavalry was not coming to Mississippi.

“Congressman Thompson looked me in the face and he said, ‘You’ve got to touch as many people as you can — you’ve got to give them the belief that this is possible,’” Mr. Colom recounted on Wednesday in his speech.

He listened. Often with his wife, Nadia, and two young daughters in tow, he crisscrossed the state. The coastal communities, the Memphis suburbs in DeSoto County, the capital, Jackson — and, one year after announcing his campaign, Mr. Colom showed up in Mound Bayou, a town of fewer than 1,500 people founded by formerly enslaved people.

It was also the place where activism helped draw attention to the brutal murder and lynching of Emmett Till in 1955 and supported his family. Mr. Colom lingered more than usual on the state’s brutal history of suppressing voting rights.

“There was no way in the world that I was going to run for United States Senate in the great state of Mississippi and not visit and campaign in Mound Bayou,” he told a gathering of a couple dozen people.

“Part of winning an election is getting people to believe it’s possible,” Mr. Colom told The Times in Mound Bayou. “The final two months,” he added, “are going to be really special.”

In the end, it all crystallized in the final few weeks.

Mr. Thompson and Black leaders like Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia kept hammering their colleagues in Washington to pay attention.

An ad skewering Ms. Hyde-Smith’s suggestion that there were alternatives to high-priced beef ricocheted across social media and became a rallying cry to “pick another senator” rather than pick another protein.

Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris, Representative James Clyburn of South Carolina, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg — they all came to Mississippi to campaign with Mr. Colom. Former President Barack Obama cut an ad supporting him. And to bolster the diverse, bipartisan coalition he needed to win, Mr. Colom even worked the line outside a rally President Trump held in Corinth for Ms. Hyde-Smith.

This past Sunday, as counties around Mississippi kept counting votes to see if he somehow had won, Mr. Colom went to church in West Point, a short drive from home, on his way back to Columbus.

He received a text message from a close friend, Jabari O. Edwards Sr.: “There are so many of our ancestors who have their blood in the ground around this state, who are now raining tears of joy down on you.”

item.title: Sister June Carpenter, the Oldest Shaker, Has Died
item.description:
Sister June Carpenter, a gentle librarian and one of three practicing members of the last active Shaker group in America, a Christian community of celibate pacifists, died on Nov. 3. She was 88.

Her death was announced by her community in a social media post that said she had been struggling with health and mobility issues, but did not provide further details.

At Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village in New Gloucester, Maine, there are 18 lovely brick and clapboard buildings bounded roadside by a white picket fence, set on a lake and 1,800 acres of farmland, woods and wetlands. But there aren’t legions of Shakers in residence.

At this point, there are only two: Brother Arnold Hadd, 70, and Sister April Baxter, who joined last year and is around 60.

Reports of the group’s extinction are a constant source of irritation to them. The oft-used newspaper headline, “The Last Shaker This or That,” particularly grates.

Most inquiries from the news media are politely declined because of reporters’ tendency to focus on the dwindling population. In one instance, media coverage may have exacerbated the situation. In 2006, after The Boston Globe published a story about the community headlined “The Last Man Standing,” one of its members, Brother Wayne Smith, fell in love with the reporter and left.

Yet the public is welcome; one never knows who might be a prospective convert.

The Shaker ideology of pacifism, celibacy and communal living — and of a loving God who embraces both genders, or a Mother-Father spirit, as it is called — beckons many these days. Would-be novices are not uncommon. As Stacey Chase, the Boston Globe reporter, noted in her story, the village can receive as many as 70 inquiries a year. But not many applicants can commit.

Perhaps that is why Sabbathday Lake has such a robust community of Shaker-adjacents and friends: paid workers and volunteers who maintain the museum, help with the farm work — there are some 200 sheep and a few cows — tend to the herb garden and its harvest, offer workshops and preside over the sales of packaged herbs, teas, yarn, furniture, candles and other goodies in the gift shop and online store. Sunday services at the Meeting House are open to all, not just the members.

A bit of history: The Shakers landed in North America in 1774 after fleeing England, where they had been persecuted for their separatist beliefs — notably their opposition to the hierarchy of the Anglican Church — and their concept of a dual-gendered God. They earned a reputation as the Shaking Quakers because of the ecstatic movements they practiced in their worship. It was a slur, but the name stuck. Those swirling dances went out of favor decades ago, though Shakers still clap and stomp a bit, as various hymns require, during the Sunday meeting.

The Sabbathday Lake community, established in 1783, was one of 11 Shaker orders in the U.S. The numbers soon swelled to 15, with some 5,000 members spread between them. In the mid-19th century, the Sabbathday Lake family, like other Shaker communities, adopted a spiritual name for itself, Chosen Land. At the time, as Jeannine Lauber wrote in “Chosen Faith, Chosen Land: The Untold Story of America’s 21st-Century Shakers” (2009), it was the smallest and poorest of all the communities. Yet it outlasted them all.

When Ms. Carpenter first visited the village in the summer of 1988, she was 49; a friend took her to the dedication of its new library. In college, she had been drawn to stories of people who had religious vocations, and she felt that she, too, wanted to give her life to God. When she learned that the community needed help cataloging its archive for the new library, she volunteered to help, and felt so at home that she asked to be considered for membership.

After Sabbathday Lake’s head curator, David Richards, interviewed her, he declared, “If the meek are to inherit the earth, she will get the whole thing!”

Sister June may have been shy, but she had a quiet, arch sense of humor and, as the announcement of her death noted, a vast knowledge of the British royal family. In addition to working as a librarian, she tended the gardens and assisted in the kitchen.

Jere DeWaters, a retired professor of photography at the University of Maine at Augusta, spent eight years at Sabbathday Lake, starting in 1986, documenting the family. He recalled Sister June’s work at the renovated library — once the village’s schoolhouse — cataloging its extensive collection of manuscripts, photographs, journals and other written material that is a treasure trove for scholars.

“She was naturally shy, but had a wonderful smile when she looked up at the camera,” Mr. DeWaters said. “Not an outgoing person at all, but she did not miss a beat. One of the quiet ones, I think the old saying goes.”

As Sister June told Ms. Lauber, “I am the last and the least of the community at the moment, and I’m very happy in that position. If I get into a position where I’m head of something, like when I was head cataloger at the library where I used to work, I feel uncomfortable and insecure. But I can cope with being little and low. It helps with the humility that we are striving for.”

The Shakers are known for their faith, their furniture and their vast hymnody: “Simple Gifts,” often referred to by its opening line, “’Tis a gift to be simple,” is one of the best-known Shaker hymns. Sister June said she related most to another one:

Great I, little i, Great I can see.

Little i is pretty i, so little I will be.

June Carpenter was born on June 15, 1938, in Boston, the only child of Florence (Blanchard) Carpenter and Sydney Carpenter, a lawyer in private practice who went on to serve in the State Legislature.

She grew up in Brookline, in a religious family. They were regulars at the Federated Church, which combines a number of Protestant denominations, including American Baptist and Congregationalist.

One day, on a trip to Boston, she recalled having a spiritual awakening as she observed the crowds. “I could see that God was within each of them,” she told Ms. Lauber. “I’ve always remembered that — that God must be inside everyone in some way, whether they realize it or not.”

The feeling faded, she said, but the insight did not: “You can’t stay on the mountaintop forever. Like the Shakers say, ‘You have to come down into the valley,’ that’s where most of life is.”

After studying library science at Simmons College (now Simmons University) in Boston, she earned a master’s degree in 1964 and then went to work as a librarian for the Brookline Public Library.

Her father had died when she was 15, and she lived with her mother until her mother’s death in 1985.

Shakers are buried without individual markers, though fellow members note the deaths in the journals they keep of their daily lives. The cemetery at Sabbathday Lake has just one gravestone. It reads simply, “Shakers.”

Sister June, with typical modesty, requested no funeral service or visiting hours.
